articles.title: Indonesia’s huge peat fires burn underground – so we still don’t know just how much carbon they have released
articles.author: Ailish Graham, Research Fellow, School of Earth and Environment, University of Leeds
paras: At the peak of Indonesia’s 2026 wildfire season, we were in Palangka Raya, a city of 300,000 people surrounded by dense peatland rainforest. Smoke covered the city in a thick yellow haze. Between mid-September and mid-October, we recorded air pollution levels equivalent to smoking about 14 cigarettes per day. On the worst days, that rose to around 30.

Our colleague Sanz Rio Griffio Limin is from the region and works at Cimtrop, a peatland research centre at the local university. “This year the fires are the worst in my lifetime,” he told us. “I am 41, and I have never seen this kind of smoke and fires.”
Unlike most wildfires, peatland fires burn beneath the ground as well as above it. These underground fires can smoulder for weeks or months and are notoriously difficult to extinguish.
Peat has accumulated carbon from dead plants over thousands of years. When it burns, that carbon is released into the atmosphere. The deeper the fire burns, the more carbon it releases.
Indonesia has wildfires every year, but they’re significantly more intense in El Niño years like this one, when there is less rain and the ground dries out further.

The country last experienced wildfires on this scale in 2015, another El Niño year. In September and October that year, Indonesia’s peat fires were releasing carbon dioxide faster than the entire European Union.

But estimates of emissions from these fires remain uncertain because we have surprisingly few direct measurements of how deeply the peat burns. That’s why one of us (Maria) travelled to Palangka Raya to join an international team of researchers measuring how much peat these fires consume and how much carbon they emit, alongside colleagues at Cimtrop, where our co-author Kitso is based.
Measuring the hidden fires

Burning peat has a particularly intense smell, which penetrated even through our face masks and other protective gear. That smell, and the wall of heat and smoke, would hit us the moment we arrived and stepped out of an air-conditioned car.
We had to be constantly vigilant for unseen underground fires and the risk of falling into a peat fire pit. Surface fires would sometimes spontaneously ignite within a few feet of our team.

The scale of the burning was extraordinary. Reaching some sites meant driving for up to 45 minutes along narrow clay tracks through an almost post-apocalyptic landscape. At the sites, fires had consumed peat underground, burning away tree roots and causing them to collapse.

Previous research suggests the water level needs to remain within about 40 centimetres of the peat surface to reduce fire risk. This year, we measured water tables between 2 and 4 metres below the surface – leaving huge layers of dry peat available to burn.

Across ten sites, we used drones and ground surveys to measure how deeply the peat had burned and estimate how much had been consumed by fire. We also collected soil samples and recorded greenhouse gas emissions from burned and unburned peat. At active fires, we measured gases released by smouldering peat, including carbon dioxide and methane, and invisible but toxic air pollution particles.

The impacts of Indonesian peat fires extend far beyond areas that burn. Smoke is transported across borders, affecting millions of people across south-east Asia, disrupting daily life and causing widespread health problems. In years like 2015 or 2026, Indonesia’s peat fires are also one of the largest sources of carbon emitted into the atmosphere, anywhere in the world.

However, estimates remain uncertain because we still don’t fully understand how burn depth and emissions vary under different peat conditions. Measurements from our fieldwork this year will help improve these estimates and strengthen smoke forecasting systems in Indonesia and surrounding countries.

We also helped local researchers deploy an additional 25 low-cost air pollution particle sensors to track smoke exposure across urban and rural areas close to peatland environments during future fire seasons.

The peat fires and haze crisis in Indonesia are largely a human-made disaster caused by peatlands being drained and degraded, making them more vulnerable to fires during droughts. Restoration can reduce this risk by raising the water table and rewetting the peat, for example, through wells or by blocking drainage canals.

These measures can reduce the number of fires. However, restoration cannot fully restore the fire resistance of intact peatlands. Protecting remaining intact peatlands while restoring those that have already been drained and degraded is our best opportunity to reduce future fire risk, protect communities from hazardous smoke and preserve globally important carbon stores.

Ailish Graham receives funding from UK Research and Innovation. This work was funded by a NERC Urgency Grant, it brought together a team from CIMTROP, University of Palangka Raya, London School of Economics, Liverpool John Moores University and University of Leeds.
Kitso Kusin works for the organization (university).

articles.title: If politicians really want to cut heating bills they need to trust in green energy – businesses already are
articles.author: Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer in Economics, Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster University
paras: This year’s United Nations climate summit, Cop31, ended in Antalya without a deal.
It appears that the world’s politicians and policy makers have collectively moved on from building a global coalition against climate change, just as its effects are becoming impossible to ignore.
Yet the public have not stopped worrying. In a 2025 global Ipsos survey, 64% of adults said failing to act on climate change would hurt future generations.
And in 2026 around 60% of American adults think global efforts will not be enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

But perhaps the biggest hurdle to making more climate-friendly changes is the current cost-of-living crisis. It appears to be politically difficult to tell cash-strapped voters to be more environmentally friendly.

Opponents of policies tackling climate change, including British and European right-wing parties and Donald Trump, seem to have effectively persuaded a majority of the public that it is impossible to make climate-friendly choices and keep your bills down. In 2026, 62% of the UK public expected net zero – Britain’s route to climate neutrality – to increase their bills in the short run.
Voters often tend to overestimate how much they would lose from a carbon tax, and to underestimate how much others care.
But despite this, people are starting to notice that climate action cannot be blamed for an economic and environmental crisis fuelled by gas and petrol prices.
The 62% share of voters who think net zero increases their bills is the lowest on record. And 51% expect net zero to be good for the economy in the long run – only 24% think it will hurt it.

Politicians are right to be careful about what voters will accept. French president Emmanuel Macron has learned the hard way, after ten years of public protests, that taxing petrol is unpopular. In Milan, some voters owning polluting cars said they were likely to vote for the far right when the city banned their vehicles from the city centre.
But very few politicians make the point that the cost-of-living crisis would be much worse without green policy.
Cost-of-living crisis is a fossil fuel crisis
In 2021, Russia supplied around 40% of the EU’s pipeline gas imports. Scrambling to replace these imports with liquefied gas from Qatar and the US has sent energy prices through the roof.

Because of its past dependency on Russian fossil fuels, Europe now pays around ten times more than the US for the same quantity of gas. These high prices have hurt the economy and pushed up inflation.
Every unit of electricity generated by wind turbines, solar panels and nuclear power plants cuts consumer bills.

Those resources saved £5.9 billion in gas imports for the UK at the start of the Iran conflict when shipping was blocked through the Strait of Hormuz. Every time no gas is needed to produce electricity, prices come down.

Significant economic damage can be caused by ignoring this. It has been clear for some time now that the future is made of electric cars and batteries. Yet European carmakers still lobby for a perpetual delay of the transition.
This strategy is costing jobs today, having transformed Europe’s leading carmakers into global laggards.
And it also hurts consumers. The world’s cheapest electric cars are made in China. EU efforts to protect what remains of its car industry using tariffs mean they cost consumers 45% more.
Britain has so far avoided the extra cost. But the EU is pushing it to impose similar tariffs.
Business is investing in green energy

But global investors are not as backward-looking as governments. This year, green energy investment is expected to reach US$2.2 trillion (£1.68 trillion) – almost double the investment in fossil fuels, and double the global investment in artificial intelligence. More than 90% of large-scale renewable investment in 2025 was cheaper than the cheapest fossil fuel alternative.
The same self-interested approach could apply to ordinary citizens.
An electric car costs less to run than a petrol one. But delays in the transition mean there are still too few charging points to make it practical for everyone.

Another factor is that in England, for instance, road congestion is taking an increasing toll on the economy, and this primarily affects motorists. Even in the US, where public transport accounts for less than 1% of journeys, when subways are not working, these few passengers switching to the car increase road congestion by 47%.
Pro-car lobbies do try to block investment in walkable cities and public transport. Will they take responsibility for the projected 85% increase in British road congestion by 2040?

Migration is very high on voters’ list of concerns, higher than any other in some British polls. And the consequences of climate change, such as flooding and high temperatures, are among the top reasons people leave their home countries. Without international cooperation on issues like water and energy, the flow of people wanting to escape poverty to live in less affected countries is likely to go up.
We live in an ageing world, and it appears that people are increasingly scared of change. The global mood feels protectionist and as crises accumulate, many want to put their own country first.
Very few environmental activists or politicians seem to speak to these instincts.

But green electricity makes you independent from foreign dictators, global cooperation should make migration more manageable, and many of our current problems come from ignoring climate change, not from trying to address it.

articles.title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
articles.author: AJ White, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, Indiana University
paras: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.
My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.
Archaeological sites forming in a modern community

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure. Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding, including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes. Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials.

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years. Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories.

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly. In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes.

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow.” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.
The past and future of climate change
To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “I’m not going to abandon my house. It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding, but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage. I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.
If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost, and some left.

Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as sudden massive floods. But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.

Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.
Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.

articles.title: Climate diplomacy is stuck – these three big changes would get it moving again
articles.author: Jan Selby, Professor of International Politics and Climate Change, University of Leeds
paras: The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, held in Antalya, Turkey, was being branded “possibly the worst Cop in history” even before its sorry conclusion.

I was there, and the conference was badly managed from start to finish: initial traffic jams and queues sapped energy and goodwill, while the final plenary was one embarrassment after another, with the summit president sniping at the UN’s climate chief (to audible gasps from delegates), and the closing “Antalya pact” being comprehensively rejected.

This sad outcome was not merely the fault of the conference’s Turkish-Australian presidency, however. The bigger issue is that climate diplomacy is stuck – and has been for several years. Structural changes are required, three in particular.
1. Climate finance is not an optional extra
First, climate finance – money provided to developing countries to help them tackle climate change – has to be increased, in particular public, grant-based finance from developed states.

This may seem an odd place to start for those weaned on the mainstream western media, where most accounts of Cop31’s failure focused on the stand off over fossil fuels. But climate finance is not an optional extra under the Paris agreement: it is the glue that holds the entire arrangement together. Ensuring adequate finance flows is one of the agreement’s three main stated aims (alongside limiting global temperature rises and supporting adaptation). And these flows are meant to progressively increase in line with mitigation ambitions and adaptation needs.

But in recent years they have not. At Cop29 in Baku, an ambitious new finance goal was planned. But instead, the conference saw a pushed-through decision that failed to offer the “progression beyond previous efforts” required by Paris and drew widespread condemnation from developing states. Nigeria termed the deal “an insult” to the UN Climate Convention.

Actual country pledges and disbursements have been falling short too. This year has seen a 70% drop in total developed country finance pledges. Meanwhile, the UK is cutting its development assistance to 0.3% of gross national income, while halving its climate finance.

The consequences have been profound. By no coincidence, within a year of the finance debacle in Baku the other side of the global climate bargain had unravelled too. The 2025 round of national mitigation plans were barely more ambitious than their previous iterations, mostly late, and collectively non-compliant with the goals of the Paris agreement.

Cop31 continued this pattern. On the conference’s eve, EU Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra declared the prospects for additional climate finance “dead in the water”. New developed world pledges for the Adaptation Fund, which helps countries prepare for and cope with the effects of climate change, totalled just US$50 million, less than half the cost of a single F-35 fighter jet.

The predictable result was deadlock on most key negotiation tracks. Indeed, for many developing countries, as well as NGOs, it was above all this climate finance issue – and not the question of whether “fossil fuels” should be named or not – that most underpinned their rejection of the Antalya pact.

The lesson should be clear: to unblock future climate summits, vastly improved finance offerings will be needed from developed countries. And that means that money will have to be diverted from elsewhere, including from the US$2.9 trillion being spent globally on militaries and war.
2. Climate coalitions need to become alliances
More money will not be enough though. Sharper political strategies are also needed, ones that are appropriate to a geopolitically fractured world and to tackling fossil fuel interests.

Cop30 in Belém, Brazil, brought a big step forward on this, with its recognition that “coalitions of the willing” are needed to overcome the UN’s consensus rules. Right now, these rules effectively give fossil fuel-dependent countries a veto on meaningful action. This led to a new process explicitly focused on “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, which began with a 57-country summit in Santa Marta, Colombia, in early 2026.

The risk, though, is that such coalitions just become new talking shops, and lack teeth. The “national roadmaps” that countries in the Santa Marta coalition are producing seem to illustrate this: the first wave of published roadmaps contains not a single new major policy commitment.

But other coalitions show us what might be possible. On the greenhouse gas methane (the focus of my current research), a powerful network of international partnerships, NGOs, funders and regulatory initiatives has transformed policy and practice over the last five years.

And building on the EU’s world-leading methane regulation, this coalition is now constructing a global marketplace that rewards cleaner producers with preferential market access, in order to help drive down methane emissions.

To really work, however, both this and other such coalitions will need commitment, regulation and enforcement. Voluntary initiatives will not be enough. And over time, such ad hoc “climate clubs” will need to transform into something much firmer – binding, treaty-based climate alliances.
3. Public pressure and protest matter

Last, it should be stressed that progress in international climate politics is not the responsibility of diplomats alone. Whatever they achieve, or do not, always reflects diverse lobbying and social pressures.

And sadly, on this front there has been a sharp regression. Since a peak in 2020, mass climate activism has largely died out. Media coverage of climate change has declined worldwide. And, spurred on by the Trump administration and war, fossil fuel interests are ascendant.
These things will only be changed through education, mobilisation and a widespread taking to the streets.

As Tasneem Essop, executive director of the NGO Climate Action Network, put it during an early Cop31 press conference: “We cannot give up on multilateralism … But if we can’t win back home, we cannot expect to win things in this space.”
Jan Selby receives funding from the European Research Council. He is a member of the Green Party of England and Wales.

articles.title: The efficiency paradox: why greener AI means more waste
articles.author: Benjamin Selwyn, Professor of International Relations and International Development, Department of International Relations, University of Sussex
paras: AI is increasingly being promoted as a solution to climate change. It can help companies use less fuel, reduce waste and make production more efficient.

For example, AI can help delivery companies plan more efficient routes, reducing the fuel they use and the emissions they produce. Similar savings could be made across other industries and transport networks, potentially reducing the overall environmental impact. But greater efficiency can also encourage more consumption.

AI is being promoted as a climate solution and as a driver of competitiveness, productivity and economic growth. The World Trade Organization estimates that the widespread adoption of AI could increase global trade by around 40% by 2040. This is generally presented as a benefit.

But there is an obvious contradiction here. If AI makes firms more efficient and profitable, it encourages further investment and expansion. Successful firms do not use productivity gains to produce less, but to expand and to make greater profits.
When these dynamics are generalised across the economy, the result is more production, transportation, resource extraction, consumption and ultimately more environmental destruction.

This is capitalism’s efficiency paradox, known as the Jevons paradox. According to William Stanley Jevons, a 19th-century English economist, any increase in resource efficiency generates an increase in long-term resource consumption, rather than a decrease.

New technologies can help businesses produce more goods using less energy, materials and labour. But by making production cheaper and faster, they can also encourage businesses to make and sell more, increasing the total amount of resources that people use.

Industrial efficiency gains have been a defining feature of capitalism since the Industrial Revolution. Steam-powered textile mills and coal mines in the late 18th century, the Bessemer steel process (making steel by blowing air through molten iron) in the 19th century, and Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th all dramatically increased efficiency.

Yet none of these efficiency gains reduced society’s overall consumption of resources. Rather, they underpinned successive waves of industrial expansion, fossil-fuel use and environmental degradation.
My research shows how digital technologies provide a historical example of this dynamic.

For decades, improvements in computers, telecommunications and data storage have allowed companies to spread different stages of production across several countries. They can now use real-time digital networks to share information and coordinate manufacturing and trade around the world.

These technologies have made possible today’s highly integrated global supply chains, allowing firms to source components from thousands of suppliers and move goods across continents with extraordinary speed and precision.
The environmental consequences are immense.

Digital technologies have helped companies produce and sell more goods around the world. This has increased the demand for raw materials, pollution from transport and damage to the natural environment. International trade in goods is now linked to around 30% of threats to the world’s species

Rather than reversing these trends, AI is deepening them. It is making supply chains faster, more responsive and more geographically extensive. From a business perspective, this is progress. Environmentally, it accelerates ecological breakdown.
Cleaner technology, more fossil fuels

The same contradiction can be seen in the energy sector. Much discussion of AI and green technology assumes that cleaner technologies replace dirtier ones. Yet, as the historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz shows, new energy systems tend to accumulate on top of rather than substitute for each other.

Wood, coal, oil, gas and renewables have largely been added to one another rather than replacing one another. Green technologies are making fossil-fuel industries more efficient, rather than replacing them.
Many of the technologies being promoted as climate solutions, including AI, are actually accelerating the extraction of fossil fuels that is driving climate change.

In Guyana, since commercial oil production began in 2019, the country has become one of the world’s fastest-growing producers of oil, with targets to produce 1.3 million barrels per day by 2027. AI-enabled drilling and “geosteering” – the real-time adjustment of a well’s path to keep it within oil-bearing rock – are increasing the rate of oil extraction.

So, can a technology designed to increase productivity, competitiveness and growth solve a crisis rooted in relentless profit-oriented expansion of production and consumption on a finite planet? Until that question is confronted, greener AI is likely to make ecological destruction more efficient rather than bring it to an end.
Benjamin Selwyn works for the University of Sussex.

articles.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
articles.author: Suvrat Dhanorkar, Associate Professor of Operations Management, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.
Gaps in climate science grow

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars.

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.
What this means for supply chains

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.
And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.
What it means for consumers

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year.
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026.
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.

articles.title: Prepaid electricity can make bills more predictable, but not necessarily more affordable
articles.author: Destenie Nock, Alex Hills Career Development Associate Professor of Engineering and Public Policy, Civil and Environmental Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: The last house I rented in Massachusetts had an oil heating tank that cost US$800 each time my roommates and I wanted to refill it. If the tank ran out, there was no heat in the home, and we had to pay extra for an emergency refill and for someone to relight the pilot. A full tank of oil could last up to a month and a half – but only if we kept the heat at 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius) when we were home and cut it off when we went to work.
Where I live now, in Pennsylvania, we use natural gas and pay afterward, based on our use. It amounts to $200 to $400 monthly – and lets us keep our heat around 70 F (21 C).

Prepaying for heat in Massachusetts certainly made me more aware of how much heating a home cost, but it didn’t make energy cheaper or help me live according to modern standards. Instead, I got used to wearing my winter coat indoors. This is still a concern for many: As winter 2026 approached, some families in Maine that have oil heat had their kids sleep in snowsuits to use less fuel and keep costs down.

Most electricity companies bill for energy already used – like the natural gas company I have in Pennsylvania. But in Maryland, Baltimore Gas and Electric is proposing a prepaid electricity program, similar to my Massachusetts oil setup.

As an energy affordability researcher studying how people change their habits to use less energy when it’s expensive, the real question for me is what this type of payment system would mean for customers. Helping households manage electricity bills is different from ensuring they can afford to use enough energy at home to keep themselves safe.

BGE, which serves approximately 1.3 million electric customers, asked Maryland Public Service Commission members to approve a prepaid program for customers in July 2026. The company says this would help people keep a better handle on their energy spending.

Rather than getting a monthly bill, customers who opted into the plan would make an initial $40 payment toward future electricity use. They could then monitor their power usage and get alerts when balances run low.

The utility’s vice president of regulatory policy and strategy, John Frain, told the Maryland Public Service Commission that prepaid customers wouldn’t have to pay security deposits to open new accounts and wouldn’t have to worry about late payment or reconnection fees if service were disconnected because they weren’t able to pay their bills.

For customers with unpaid balances of up to $1,000, the company would have 25% of each prepayment applied to previous debts and 75% go toward future electricity costs. The company expects to save a yet-undetermined amount of money on collection efforts.
Consumer advocates warn that prepaid billing could cause problems for customers while making life easier for the utility company.
For instance, people on fixed incomes, such as Social Security, could experience increased mental stress because of frequent fears their electricity might be cut off.

They also might make significant changes in their lifestyles: A 2014 study in New Zealand found customers who prepaid for their electricity rationed their own power by, for instance, turning on an electric water heater only every third day and taking cold showers on other days.

Because Maryland prepaid customers would pay the same electricity rates as everyone else, any bill savings would likely come from living without many of the basic services electricity brings to modern life.

The company’s response to this concern is that while customers whose balance gets to zero will be disconnected – as soon as the next day – they’ll have an easier time getting reconnected. Once people add $15 to their account, power can be restored in less than 30 minutes.

But even short disconnections can cause big problems. For people dependent on electric-powered medical devices, such as breathing equipment or home dialysis machines, getting disconnected can injure or kill them. Without the power to charge a phone or power a Wi-Fi router, some people may have trouble getting alerts about their balance or making payments to turn their electricity back on.
Keeping the lights on, even in hardship

Under traditional billing, Maryland law gives customers protections against rapid disconnections. When people are late paying their bills, utilities have to notify them of the overdue balance and give them at least 14 days to pay before cutting off power – a period during which they can still use electricity.
This delay gives people a chance to make payment arrangements and seek financial assistance, such as from the state’s Office of Home Energy Programs.
Applying to that office allows customers to request an additional 55-day reprieve from disconnection, which can help families stay connected during extreme weather events.
In August 2019, BGE conducted a trial run of the prepaid system with 527 customers.

An independent analysis found that power disconnections were often shorter – five hours on average – for prepaid customers than for customers who were billed later for the power they used, whose power was off for an average of 9.4 days. But 10% of prepaid customers had their power cut off at some point during the test period, compared with just 1% of those in the traditional billing program.

The trial run generated some positive outcomes for customers: 61% of the participants said they had better control over their energy bills by being able to decide when and how much to prepay, and 34% said the program’s feature of progressively paying off overdue bills helped them.
However, 41% of participants left before the program formally ended in November 2020. Among those who left, one-third didn’t like making frequent payments, and 23% felt their energy cost more.
A way to help consumers without also hurting them?
BGE told Maryland officials that the prepaid program is “not intended as a cost-savings program for customers.”
The company says its prepay program offers customers online tools to monitor their energy use and the option to make payments when it’s financially convenient.
But BGE customers can already do both of those things online.

And a utility that cuts people off for running out of credit has less incentive to help customers actually afford sufficient levels of energy to live their lives. That’s because investor-owned utilities generally don’t earn money on selling more electricity, but rather on building and maintaining power lines and substations. In fact, if systemwide energy use drops – due to mild weather or people choosing to use less energy – and the utility collects less than its approved revenue target, then Maryland law lets it charge customers more so the utility can cover its costs and still make a profit.

The Maryland Public Service Commission will decide on BGE’s proposal in January 2027. Its ruling on this prepaid electricity system will determine whether people who seek greater control over their monthly bills would have to give up legal protections that help customers continue to meet their basic energy needs without sacrificing their health and safety during financial hardships.

Destenie Nock is on the board of Clean Energy Works. She has previously received funding from NSF, RK Mellon Foundation, the Sloan Foundation, and the Environmental Protection Agency. She has advocated for disconnection protections for households in regulatory filings and has worked as an expert witness for the AGO in Massachusetts. She is the CEO of Peoples Energy Analytics.

articles.title: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
articles.author: Francesco Grillo, Academic Fellow, Department of Social and Political Sciences, Bocconi University
paras: The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.
Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration (issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).
We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.
Francesco Grillo is Director of the think tank Vision.

articles.title: Swimming spots won’t get official bathing water status if they’re tricky to clean under England’s new rules
articles.author: Karolina Krupska, PhD Candidate, Environmental Science and Water Quality, University of Reading
paras: If a beach or riverside spot in England is popular with swimmers, anyone can apply for it to be given official bathing status. Official status means that the water will be tested and monitored regularly, and given a rating from “excellent” to “poor”.

Now, though, popular swimming spots can be refused official bathing water status in England if government agencies judge that meeting minimum water quality standards will be too difficult or disproportionately expensive.

Until recently, official bathing status was granted to a place being used by large numbers of swimmers – the water did not have to be clean before designation. A site could be granted official bathing status while being classified as “poor”, with recommendations to avoid swimming there. Bathing status designation and water quality classification were separate.

But official status requires regular Environment Agency testing for bacteria that indicate faecal contamination, with up to 20 samples taken during the bathing season, from May to September. Further requirements include information for swimmers and duties to investigate and address pollution.

England’s new rules, in force since May 2026, have added a check before official designation. Can water realistically be improved to at least “sufficient” status without disproportionate expense? A polluted site can still be designated if it passes that assessment, but designation must be refused if ministers accept that improvement is not feasible or is considered too expensive.

If status is refused by the Environment Agency (with final decisions being made by Defra, the government’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs), who will tackle the water pollution and keep swimmers informed?
Designation driving improvement

Church Cliff beach in Lyme Regis, Dorset, was first designated as a bathing water in 1988. Its water was classified as “poor” in 2015. Routine testing for bacteria in water stopped when the beach lost its official status in 2016 due to so few people swimming there.

But some people did continue to swim at Church Cliff beach. For two years, campaigners fought to restore its designation as an official bathing spot and secure action on pollution. The town council supported the public call for redesignation and subsequent water quality monitoring. People were still swimming at this beach and when designation returned in 2024, testing for bacteria resumed and pollution information signs followed. But the water had not been cleaned up in the interim and this site was classified as “poor” again that year.

Designation could help drive the work needed to help clean up water pollution. After redesignation of Church Cliff beach, the Environment Agency drew up a plan in 2025 to reduce sewage discharges, fix leaking pipes and tackle farm pollution. Utility company South West Water committed to sewage upgrades, while the town council worked with the Environment Agency to set up a group to oversee improvements.
For new applications, this process will not be possible if it is judged that improving water quality is not feasible or would be disproportionately expensive.

The government argues that limited resources should go where they can deliver results. It also wants to avoid giving swimmers false reassurance about places that cannot meet minimum standards. Yet Defra’s original 2024 consultation on reforming bathing water regulations acknowledged that refusing designation could discourage investment at polluted sites. Whether that happens will depend on how decisions are made and what follows.

These decisions depend on understanding pollution sources. At East Looe in Cornwall, the bathing water was rated “poor” in 2015. After heavy rain, the River Looe can carry runoff from farmland and sewage from overflowing sewers miles downstream to the beach.

Different sources call for different measures. Upstream in Liskeard, South West Water built two underground tanks to store wastewater during storms and reduce sewage spills into Looe Bay. This was part of a bathing water scheme completed in spring 2015. Cornwall Wildlife Trust offered farmers grants for better roofing and drainage to keep farm waste out of streams during heavy rain. In 2019, East Looe’s bathing water earned its first “good” rating, which it still held in 2025.
The new rules under scrutiny

The new bathing water status application process includes water quality checks before designation and, where necessary, an assessment of whether improvements are feasible. But the published guidance does not specify how thoroughly each pollution source will be investigated.
The watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection welcomed the reforms. It has also called for clear reasons and public involvement.

Defra’s guidance on bathing water applications says decisions will be explained. Details of the feasibility assessment will follow. It remains unclear whether the method will follow the watchdog’s advice on calculating cleanup costs.

The environmental campaign charity Surfers Against Sewage is challenging the rules in court. Surfers Against Sewage argues that the new rules undermine the protections that designation is meant to provide. The High Court granted permission for the challenge to proceed in October 2026, with a hearing scheduled for February 2027.

Any refusal should explain which pollution sources were investigated, why cleanup was judged infeasible or too expensive, and what could allow reconsideration. It should clarify which monitoring will continue and who will inform swimmers. This would help people make informed choices and communities track whether pollution is being tackled.

For swimmers and river users, the consequences go far beyond a place on an official list. Without clear warnings, people may unknowingly enter polluted water and develop infections. These can cause diarrhoea and vomiting and, in severe cases, life-threatening complications such as kidney failure. Refusal should never mean abandoning efforts to improve water quality.
Karolina Krupska is the founder of the Water Science Foundation.

articles.title: As US farms consolidate, small-town America has been losing out
articles.author: Leland Glenna, Professor of Rural Sociology and Science, Technology, and Society, Penn State
paras: The farmer-poet Wendell Berry once described a dystopian world where society is singularly directed toward “the objective” – a relentless drive for industrial extraction that leads to the destruction of nature and communities.

The idea captured Berry’s concerns about the industrialization of agriculture and the expansion of natural resource extraction that became prominent across rural America in the latter decades of the 20th century.

Over nine decades, Berry watched how agribusinesses’ and farm owners’ pursuit of productive efficiency and maximum profits led to machines and synthetic chemicals replacing human farm labor, and the replacement of diversified farms with monocropping and concentrated animal-feeding operations. Across the U.S., he saw small farms disappear, often consolidated into vast corporate businesses with absent owners.
What gets lost in this pursuit of production and profit, he noted, are community, human dignity and flourishing, natural beauty and ecological well-being.
As agriculture researchers and rural sociologists, we, like Berry, have seen how the industrialization of agriculture has changed the face of rural America and hollowed out its communities.

Once-thriving main streets in rural towns have slowly lost their businesses, with fewer farm-related jobs to keep local residents in the area. Machine dealers and suppliers of farm input such as seeds, fertilizer and pesticides have disappeared. Local grocery stores have been replaced by gas station convenience stores. Schools have shrunk or consolidated with the population decline. Hospitals have closed.
This “unsettling of America,” in Berry’s words, shows that the farm economy and the rural economy no longer rise and fall together. Rural communities continue to decline despite farm booms and busts.
Losing farming’s rural economy multiplier effect
Since the late 1940s, the number of farmers in the U.S. has plummeted by nearly 90%, falling from 5.9 million in 1948 to only 715,000 by 2025.

During the same period, the agricultural workforce has shifted from mostly farm owners – about 78% – with a few hired hands in 1948 to one today where most of the work is done by farm laborers, about 68% of the workforce. This means profits from farming mainly flow to a small number of farm owners, while the people doing the farm work are paid much less.
The loss of small, owner-operated farms, where a farm family could make a living, is one reason many rural communities have lost population over the past century.

In prior eras, farming energized rural communities as money circulated in the rural economy, supporting rural businesses and populations – what is termed a “multiplier effect.” Today, local suppliers and services are harder to find, and farm profits instead flow to owners outside the community.

Agriculture today resembles capital-intensive natural resource extraction, like mining, where a small number of very profitable businesses operate most acres in the county. Such farms employ few people at low wages, and profits accrue to distant landlords and investment firms. This shift further reinforces rural decline.

The farm economy of the 21st century does little to create additional jobs in rural America. An analysis of 11 counties in Iowa found that every US$1 million of agricultural sales creates 2.4 total farm jobs and 1.6 spin-off jobs in other nonfarm businesses, for a total of four new jobs.

By contrast, healthcare creates 10 new jobs and construction creates seven new jobs in all for every $1 million in sales. Both pay good wages, which keeps rural people from leaving and helps rural economies thrive. Both also create more spin-off jobs. In short, agriculture produces profits for the company, whereas healthcare and construction produce good-paying jobs for rural residents.
More small farms can help communities thrive
In the mid-1940s, the U.S. Senate commissioned two studies on the social impacts of economic concentration and corporate monopolies.

In one, Walter Goldschmidt, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, described two agricultural communities in California, one with a few large farms and the other with numerous smaller farms. He evaluated the social qualities of each and found that the community with more small farms had a higher standard of living and quality of life than the community with a few large farms.

The other study, overseen by Columbia sociology professor C. Wright Mills, compared urban manufacturing areas in the Midwest. It found that locations with many small companies had a more robust economic life, with higher socioeconomic well-being, than areas dominated by a few large firms.

Many rural sociologists have tested these findings since then. One, a Cornell study led by rural sociologist Thomas Lyson, found a way to counter the effects of farm consolidation. Using U.S. Census of Agriculture and other county-level data, it found that communities with large-scale industrial-style farms that also had politically active populations and a high percentage of people running small, independent businesses tended to have higher levels of social well-being than those without.
The effect of economic concentration
Looking at the agriculture sector in 2026, it’s clear that policymakers have not listened to the concerns raised by Berry or the rural sociologists.
According to the latest Census of Agriculture, America had fewer than 2 million farms in 2022. Fewer than 6% of those farms accounted for over three-quarters of all agricultural production.

Farms are getting larger and more specialized. Economist Jim MacDonald documented that half of all cropland in 2017 was on farms with 1,445 acres, more than double the 650 acres in 1987. Half of all dairy farms had more than 1,300 cows in 2017, up from 80 in 1987. Half of all pig farms in 1987 marketed 1,200 pigs or more – the midpoint is currently over 50,000 pigs per year.

The supply chain is also shrinking, leaving farmers with fewer choices. Today, fewer companies control more of the markets where farmers buy their fertilizers and pesticides or sell their products, which means that farmers have less control over what they can raise or sell.

For instance, just two companies accounted for 71.6% of the U.S. corn seed market in 2018-2022, and those same two companies accounted for 65.9% of the soybean seed market, according to USDA researchers. Twenty years earlier, the top two companies in those markets accounted for 47.2% of the corn seed market and 41.8% of the soybean seed market.

When four or fewer firms control 40% or more of a market, farmers tend to pay more for seeds, fertilizer and pest control and receive less for their commodities, while consumers continue to face higher prices.
Consolidation of land and commodity markets at the farm level often goes unnoticed and sometimes undocumented.

University of Iowa economist Silvia Secchi describes how changes in the U.S. Census of Agriculture in 2002 and in 2017 “obfuscates the degree of consolidation” in the farm sector by allowing farms to report up to three or four farm operators. These changes have led to the official count of over 3 million farm operators, even though there are fewer than 2 million farms.
By looking at the volume of sales, Secchi found that fewer than half of these 2 million farms produce commodities worth more than $1,000 annually.

She contends that this way of counting farmers does a double disservice to small farm operators. First, it lumps disadvantaged farmers into a group that includes retired farmers and farmland owners who might be using their land as a tax write-off. Second, when the overall farm incomes are averaged, the inclusion of these small farmers make the large, high-value farmers appear to need more federal support.
How to improve conditions in farm country
Restoring the vibrant rural farm economy of the past may be unrealistic, but some policies could at least improve conditions.

Devising new – and enforcing existing – antitrust laws to break up oligopolies and monopolies in the materials farms need, such as seeds and fertilizer, as well as in processing and trade could give farmers more choices about what to raise and where to sell it, while protecting consumers from high prices.
Right-to-repair laws could help farmers gain more control over their expensive machinery.

Farm subsidies could be directed to smaller farmers who produce food – many of whom were inspired by Berry to become farmers – rather than toward the largest farmers who produce a few commodities at a massive scale.

And finally, policymakers can develop rural policies that actually invest in the rural environment and communities, rather than simply subsidizing commodities in ways that primarily benefit the corporate owners of vast areas of farmland.

articles.title: The curious history of the huntaway, New Zealand’s unusually loud sheepdog
articles.author: Gareth Enticott, Professor of Human Geography, Cardiff University; University of Waikato
paras: Sheepdog trials don’t always take place in a field. Some take place in a pub.

Across New Zealand, “bark-ups” are a common sight at pubs and agricultural events, and feature a home-bred invention: the New Zealand huntaway dog breed. The aim of the bark-up is simple: find the dog with the best bark.

To outsiders, the spectacle raises an obvious question: why would anyone hold a competition to find the sheepdog that barks the loudest? The answer lies not just in the sheep stations of New Zealand where the huntaway was developed, but in the colonisation of New Zealand, for sheepdogs are breeds of empire. It’s something I explore in my new book.

The modern sheepdog was a Victorian invention. Queen Victoria herself was a fan of the collie, buying the best from shepherds on the England-Scotland borders. Those shepherds were at the helm of the emerging sheepdog trialling scene at the start of the 20th century.

In the process, sheepdogs came to embody Victorian moral values. The ideal dog displayed discipline, intelligence, restraint, obedience and industriousness, and perhaps most of all, silence while working – qualities that were equally applicable to the shepherd.

Organisations such as the International Sheep Dog Society reinforced these ideals. Under its influential honorary secretary, James Reid, the border collie was invented not merely as a useful farm dog but as the pinnacle of canine improvement.

Exported throughout Britain’s settler colonies, it became a breed of empire, carrying with it particular ideas about good stockmanship, moral character and agricultural modernity. Reid went so far as to describe the sheepdog as the foundation of the pastoral economy, whose intelligence and labour underpinned the success of the British empire.

Scottish settlers had already taken their sheepdogs to New Zealand in the mid-19th Century. But it would be a Northumbrian, James Lilico, who would transform New Zealand’s sheepdogs. Arriving in 1894 to work as a shepherd, he immediately sent home for his dog Captain, disappointed by the “useless mongrels” he had been given to work.

So started half a century of importing the finest sheepdogs he could source, usually championship winning trial dogs, earning him the title of the “collie king of New Zealand”. Lilico imported sheepdogs that had been bred with the quality known as “eye” (herding using an intense stare) that had become highly valued among triallists. Breeding them, Lilico championed the superiority of what he called “border dogs” in his weekly column in the New Zealand Farmer periodical.

Lilico’s actions were not universally welcomed, in particular his criticism of the sheepdogs and shepherds who worked New Zealand’s high country. For the shepherds of these regions, Lilico’s strong-eyed dogs were too slow, too delicate and insufficiently forceful. In their view, sheep needed to be moved, not mesmerised.

Their alternative was the huntaway. What marked out the huntaway from the border collie was its noise. Without fences and across wide open country, noise had become a valuable tool for shepherds. Before setting out to muster sheep, shepherds gathered their dogs and instructed them to bark. This bark up – just like those now seen in pubs – guided sheep from a distance, so by the time shepherds arrived the sheep were already on the move.

If its bark united the huntaway, their appearance did anything but. Old photographs reveal a variety of different appearances and types: from small and fluffy to larger looking collies. But as sheep farming expanded from the South Island into the hill country of the North Island, the huntaway began to evolve.

To make the huntaway more powerful to deal with stubborn Romney sheep, its voice got louder. Breeding experiments involving mastiff, rottweiler, labrador, hound and other breeds sought to improve its barking power. A bigger huntaway became more common, but even now the huntaway defies standardisation beyond its capacity to bark all day.

Crucially, while the development of New Zealand agriculture was part of a scientific “grasslands revolution”, these scientists had little to do with sheepdogs. The huntaway instead reflected the spirit of farmers, as a “practical dog for practical men”. Scientists and breed societies were kept well away in fear of ruining the dog.
Recognition and uncertainty

In 2013 the huntaway was recognised as a unique breed by the New Zealand Kennel Club, but its origins were still uncertain. Recent genetic studies show that it is related to the border collie, and other breeds imported in the 19th century. Genetic traces of the breeds used for power are harder to find, reinforcing the mythology that surrounds the breed.

It may also be that its defining feature – the bark – is not simply a New Zealand invention but an echo of its past. Back in Scotland in 1935, James Reid had given a lecture celebrating the border collie conquering all other breeds of sheepdog. Its popularity had meant that other barking sheepdogs used across Wales and southern England had no place, consigning them to history.

When James Lilico wrote about the huntaway in one of his three books, he received a letter from a shepherd in north Wales suggesting that the Huntaway sounded no different to the dog known as ci hanos, a dog that used noise to drive sheep onto the hills in the springtime.

Lilico had planned on importing one of these as part of a breeding experiment. Such an experiment might be more valuable today as the huntaway gene pool narrows: the closure of large sheep stations in New Zealand is making breeding selection a challenge. In doing so, it raises existential questions about sheepdogs themselves, because without sheep there will be no sheepdogs.
Gareth Enticott receives funding from the Welsh and UK Government.

articles.title: Panic buying? Gradual stockpiling makes for better ‘prepping’ without emptying supermarket shelves
articles.author: Sayed Elhoushy, Senior Lecturer in Marketing, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Soon after the government launched its “Be Ready” campaign, supermarket shelves were empty where the bottled water usually sits. Torches quickly went out of stock too.

Two days before the campaign launch in October, one of us (Sayed Elhoushy) argued at a Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology roundtable that households need a clear standard for what being prepared means, including how to build supplies gradually. The “gradually” is key.
In the ten days following campaign launch, sales of essentials surged. According to retail research firm Worldpanel, sales of tinned food rose by 37%, bottled water by 67% and hand sanitiser by 83%.

The Be Ready campaign asks households to stock three days of supplies, including water, tinned food, medicines and cash. It tells people what to buy, but little on when. Without guidance on timing, many households may all act on the same advice at the same time.

When shelves emptied before the first COVID lockdown, researchers at the Institute for Fiscal Studies showed the higher demand came from more households than usual buying storable goods. Shoppers can still strip a shelf, even if they all buy little amounts, at once. The anticipation of empty shelves can then raise urgency and fear. That urgency and fear change how people shop.

The past few years witnessed a series of unprecedented, concurrent and consecutive disruptions. Cost-of-living crisis, heatwaves, droughts and geopolitical tensions created uncertainty in peoples’ daily lives. When people feel unsafe, they buy more, and shortages follow, real or imagined. Research with US shoppers during COVID found that fear can override good intentions: people who wanted to shop responsibly still stockpiled when they were afraid.

Scarcity makes products more desirable and pushes people to seek more, within short notice. In the pandemic, the risk of store closures created panic. People rushed for staples, driven by fear of missing out, social conformity or herd mentality.

People do not make the best decisions when pressured. They look for short-term, smaller gains, at the expense of longer-term, better ones. Feelings of urgency shortens decision making time, but can also cause post-purchase regret. Fear of missing out, triggers anxiety and panic buying. Social media intensifies such emotions.

Prepping, or getting ready in anticipation of disruptions, can favour the privileged. Research shows that adjusting to changes takes extra space, time and money, just when rising prices are squeezing budgets. Prepping can be gendered, reflecting the already disproportionate share of domestic and care work in households.

The Be Ready checklist suggests 36 litres of drinking water for a family of four. Carrying 36kg home is an enormous challenge if you do not have a car. In minimising disruptions, and attempting to empower, it is critical that plans do not exacerbate existing vulnerabilities during crisis situations.
The UK Public Survey of Risk Perception identifies that 29% of respondents consider costs as limiting. A quarter do not want food to go out of date and end up in the bin.

Stockpiling however, does not necessarily mean more waste. Italian households bought more food during lockdown, yet waste was low, as they mostly bought non-perishables. UK households self-reported 34% less food wastage, as people planned meals, froze leftovers and cooked from what they had.
How a sense of control helps

If fear drives buying, a sense of control calms it. Research shows that shortages weaken people’s sense of control, which fuels panic buying. Uncertainty can also fuel people’s anxiety, making panic buying more likely. When many households act on the same advice in the same week, they can create the very empty shelves that unsettle others. A clear plan gives that control back.

Advice to build up supplies over a month, adding two or three items to each shop. Start with water and tinned food, then add medicines and batteries. This spreads demand for retailers, spreads the cost for households, and gives people a clear plan to follow. Information should also be provided in multiple languages, across modalities, to increase awareness about risks while making them ready.
Food literacy should come to the fore. Consumers need to understand how to look out for expiry dates and use products on a first in, first out, basis to minimise waste, engage with food preservation.

Preparedness should start at school too. A review of 61 studies shows that disaster education in schools works, but many countries do too little. Programmes work best when lessons involve families and the wider community. Children then bring the plan home, resocialising their households towards joint actions.

What the public posts online also matters as much as what government says. A study of UK shoppers during COVID found that photos of empty shelves on social media increased uncertainty about stock; many responded by buying more. Those photos can signal fear and lead to panic. Retailers can help too. Setting allocation mechanisms such as maximum purchase quantities per customer can support with matching demand and supply.
